mathgap.title: Signed 'has N more than'
mathgap.principle: Interpret statements of the form 'X has N more than Y' as the signed equation X = Y + N (or X - Y = N).
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence directly compares two people's counts using 'more than' or 'fewer than'.
mathgap.example: Treating 'X has N more than Y' as X = |Y - N|, i.e., taking an absolute value and losing the sign.

mathgap.title: Signed relational equation
mathgap.principle: For statements that equate one difference to another, such as 'the number of X that A has more than B equals the difference between C and D', translate to (A - B) = (C - D).
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence sets a difference between two people equal to a difference between another pair.
mathgap.example: Writing A - B = |C - D|, incorrectly applying absolute value on the right side.

mathgap.title: Allow negative differences
mathgap.principle: Do not assume that a 'more than' or 'difference' clause yields a positive result; keep the sign as indicated, allowing negative values when appropriate.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement includes 'fewer than' or when the computed difference could be negative.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'X has 45 fewer mangoes than Y' as X = Y + 45 instead of X = Y - 45.

mathgap.title: Model transfers as net changes
mathgap.principle: Each 'X gives N to Y' reduces X by N and increases Y by N; apply these net changes to the current counts before processing later statements.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence describes a transfer of a specific number of items from one person to another.
mathgap.example: Adding N to both X and Y, effectively moving the items in the wrong direction.

mathgap.title: Absolute count statements refer to final counts
mathgap.principle: When a problem mixes absolute count statements (e.g., 'X has N mangoes') with transfers, splits, or redistributions, treat the absolute counts as describing the final amounts after all such operations, unless the problem explicitly says otherwise.
mathgap.when_to_apply: If a problem contains both 'has N' statements and any kind of transfer or redistribution.
mathgap.example: Assuming 'X has N' describes the initial amount before transfers, leading to contradictory totals.

mathgap.title: Systematic equation solving
mathgap.principle: Represent each person as a variable and write a linear equation for every relational, transfer, split, or redistribution statement; then solve the resulting system of equations.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For any problem with multiple interrelated statements that together determine the unknown counts.
mathgap.example: Solving each statement in isolation without linking variables, missing constraints.

mathgap.title: Distinct variables for similar names
mathgap.principle: Treat each distinct name as a separate variable, even if the names look similar or share a common prefix; do not merge them.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem includes names that differ by only a few letters or share a root.
mathgap.example: Combining 'Miriam' and 'Myrtie' into a single variable, causing incorrect equations.

mathgap.title: Combined sum interpretation
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'X has N more than Y and Z combined', translate to X = (Y + Z) + N (or X - (Y + Z) = N).
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence compares one person's count to the sum of two others plus or minus a constant.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'X has N more than Y and Z combined' as X = Y + Z - N, reversing the sign.

mathgap.title: Increase by factor interpretation
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'the number of X increases by N times', interpret it as multiplication: new = old * N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence uses phrasing like 'increases by N times' or 'is N times larger'.
mathgap.example: Treating 'increases by 2 times' as new = old + 2, ignoring the multiplicative meaning.

mathgap.title: Equal split and redistribution handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'splits all the mangoes she owns equally among X and Y', treat it as the splitter ends with zero and each recipient receives half of the splitter's original amount; when a statement says 'redistribute their mangoes to ensure each has an equal amount', treat it as the two persons pool their mangoes and each ends with half of the total.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a problem includes statements about splitting all items equally among two recipients, or redistributing items between two people to achieve equal amounts.
mathgap.example: Keeping half of the mangoes for the splitter after a 'splits all ... equally' statement, or assuming each person keeps their original amount in a redistribution.

mathgap.description: Assuming positivity for 'has more than' statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: Models default to positive differences and forget that 'fewer than' or negative differences are possible.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep the sign of the difference as given; use signed equations without taking absolute values.

mathgap.description: Applying transfers in the wrong direction
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When parsing 'X gives N to Y', subtract N from X and add N to Y.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting 'increase by X times' as addition rather than multiplication
mathgap.why_it_happens: Misreading 'times' as a count rather than a factor.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Interpret 'increase by N times' as new = old * N.

mathgap.description: Treating 'X has N' as an initial count before transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: Misunderstanding the convention that absolute counts are final when transfers are present.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When transfers are present, treat 'X has N' as describing the final count after all operations, unless the problem says otherwise.

mathgap.why_it_happens: Confusing splitting (giving away all) with redistribution (pooling and sharing).
mathgap.how_to_avoid: For a split, set the splitter's final count to zero and give each recipient half of the original amount; for redistribution, set both participants to half of the sum of their pre-redistribution amounts.
